source_refs.note: Book p. 5-6: 1.4 definition of exponential function and base, natural exponential function and e, growth and decay

blocks.text: The function defined by \(f(x) = a^{x}\) for all \(x \in \mathbb{R}\), where \(a > 0\) and \(a \ne 1\), is called an exponential function. The number \(a\) is called the base of the exponential function.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why must the base satisfy \(a > 0\) and \(a \ne 1\)?
\(a = 1\): \(1^{x} = 1\) for every \(x\), a constant, nothing "exponential" about it.
\(a = 0\): \(0^{x}\) is not defined for \(x \le 0\) (e.g. \(0^{-2} = \frac{1}{0^{2}}\)).
\(a < 0\): \((-9)^{1/2} = \sqrt{-9}\) is not real, so \(a^{x}\) is not defined for all real \(x\).
With \(a > 0,\ a \ne 1\), the value \(a^{x}\) is a real number for every real \(x\).
The function \(f(x) = e^{x}\) is called the natural exponential function, where \(e\) is a number defined by

blocks.text_alt: e equals the sum, from n equals 0 to infinity, of 1 over n factorial

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
What does the sum mean? Write out the first terms (recall \(0! = 1\)):
\[e = 1 + 1 + \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{1}{6} + \dfrac{1}{24} + \cdots\]
The first five terms already give \(2.70833\ldots\), and adding more terms brings the total closer and closer to \(2.71828\ldots\). Like \(\pi\), the number \(e\) is irrational, so we always use an approximation. On a calculator, \(e^{x}\) is the key marked \(e^{x}\) (often SHIFT + ln).
The exponential functions \(f(x) = e^{x}\) and \(g(x) = 2^{x}\) represent exponential growth, while the function \(f(x) = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{x}\) represents exponential decay.

blocks.caption: Growth and decay side by side (our worked table)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Read the table down the columns. For \(2^{x}\), each step of 1 in \(x\) doubles the value: that is growth. For \(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{x}\), each step halves the value: that is decay. In general \(a > 1\) gives growth and \(0 < a < 1\) gives decay. Also notice \(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{x} = 2^{-x}\), so the two columns are the same numbers in reverse order.

blocks.caption: Power function vs exponential function (our comparison table)

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Exponential function: \(f(x) = a^{x}\), \(x \in \mathbb{R}\), with base \(a > 0\), \(a \ne 1\).
2. Natural exponential function: \(f(x) = e^{x}\), \(e = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n!} \approx 2.71828\).
3. \(a > 1\) (e.g. \(e^{x}\), \(2^{x}\)): exponential growth; \(0 < a < 1\) (e.g. \(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{x}\)): exponential decay.
4. \(\left(\frac{1}{a}\right)^{x} = a^{-x}\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Writing \(2^{-1} = -2\): a negative exponent means a reciprocal, \(2^{-1} = \frac{1}{2}\).
2. Confusing \(x^{2}\) with \(2^{x}\): they agree at \(x = 2\) and \(x = 4\) but are different functions.
3. Taking \(e = 2.7\) too early in a calculation: keep \(e\) (or the calculator value) until the last step.
